questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: What a map scale must be applied to
questions.learningObjective: State what a map scale relates
questions.stem: Nurse 01 checks whether a map scale applies to map distances, areas, or both before measuring a ward plan.

options.text: A map scale relates map distance to the corresponding ground distance.
A map scale automatically rescales every area shown on the map.
options.misconception: assumes scale applies to area without recomputing

options.text: A map scale fixes the angle between any two mapped bearings.
A map scale records the elevation of each mapped feature.

questions.explanation: A scale is a ratio of map distance to ground distance, so it must be applied to lengths, not to areas, angles, or heights. Areas need squared scale factors.
questions.hint: Apply the scale to a length first.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: A verbal scale and its equivalent fraction
questions.learningObjective: Convert a verbal scale to a representative fraction
questions.stem: Nurse 02 converts the verbal scale one centimetre to five hundred metres into a representative fraction.

options.text: The equivalent representative fraction is 1:5,000.
options.misconception: drops a zero from the conversion

options.text: The equivalent representative fraction is 1:50,000.
The equivalent representative fraction is 1:500,000.
options.misconception: adds an extra zero to the ground distance

options.text: The equivalent representative fraction is 1:500.

questions.explanation: One centimetre on the map equals five hundred metres, or fifty thousand centimetres, on the ground, giving 1:50,000. The other fractions misplace zeros or units.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Map distance converted to ground distance
questions.learningObjective: Convert map distance to ground distance
questions.stem: Nurse 03 measures 3.4 cm on a 1:25,000 map and computes the ground distance.

options.text: Therefore, the ground distance is 8.5 km.
Therefore, the ground distance is 0.085 km.
Therefore, the ground distance is 0.85 km.
Therefore, the ground distance is 85 km.

questions.explanation: Multiplying 3.4 cm by 25,000 gives 85,000 cm, which is 0.85 km. Dividing or misplacing decimals gives the tempting wrong values.
questions.hint: Multiply then convert centimetres to kilometres.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Large scale preserves detail rather than extent
questions.learningObjective: Relate scale to detail and extent
questions.stem: Nurse 04 compares a 1:10,000 map with a 1:250,000 map for a ward catchment.

options.text: The 1:250,000 map shows more detail for a small area.
options.misconception: confuses large scale with small extent

options.text: Both maps show the same detail and extent.
The 1:10,000 map covers a larger total area.
The 1:10,000 map shows more detail for a smaller area.

questions.explanation: A larger scale means a bigger ratio, so each map unit covers less ground and more detail can be shown over a smaller extent. The smaller scale covers more ground with less detail.
questions.hint: Larger ratio means smaller ground area per map unit.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Reading the property a projection preserves
questions.learningObjective: Identify the property a projection preserves
questions.stem: Nurse 05 reads that a projection preserves local angles and asks what it is called.

options.text: The projection is conformal and keeps local shapes.
The projection is equal-area and keeps sizes.
The projection is equidistant and keeps all distances.
The projection is azimuthal and keeps directions.

questions.explanation: A conformal projection preserves local angles and shapes. Equal-area, equidistant, and azimuthal projections preserve different properties.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Area error of a conformal projection at a stated latitude
questions.learningObjective: Explain area error on a conformal projection
questions.stem: Nurse 06 asks why area is badly distorted on a Mercator map near sixty degrees latitude.

options.text: Conformal projections keep area true everywhere.
Conformal projections keep angles, so area is distorted.
Conformal projections keep distances along all parallels.
Conformal projections remove all distortion at the equator.

questions.explanation: Conformal projections preserve angles, which forces area to stretch, and the stretch grows with latitude on a cylindrical projection. Keeping area true would require a different projection.
questions.hint: Angles preserved force area to change.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: What a conformal projection promises
questions.learningObjective: State what a conformal projection guarantees
questions.stem: Nurse 07 asks what a conformal projection guarantees to its users.

options.text: It preserves area across the whole map.
It preserves distance along every line.
It preserves local angles and shapes.
It preserves direction from one centre only.

questions.explanation: A conformal projection guarantees that local angles and small shapes are preserved, even though areas and some distances are distorted. It does not promise area or global distance.

provenance.author: bank-team-human-geography

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: What an equal-area projection gives up
questions.learningObjective: State what an equal-area projection sacrifices
questions.stem: Nurse 08 compares an equal-area projection with other projections.

options.text: It keeps both area and shape perfectly.
It keeps area but distorts angles only at poles.
It keeps area but stretches distances uniformly.
It keeps area while distorting shape and angle.

questions.explanation: An equal-area projection keeps every region's area proportional to reality, but shapes, angles, and distances are distorted, especially far from standard lines. No projection keeps both area and shape perfectly.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Why a cylindrical projection inflates high latitudes
questions.learningObjective: Explain high-latitude inflation on cylindrical projections
questions.stem: Nurse 09 asks why Greenland looks huge on a Mercator map.

options.text: Cylindrical projection stretches east-west spacing at high latitudes.
The scale bar is printed too small for polar regions.
High latitudes have genuinely larger landmasses.
The projection preserves area, so shapes must stretch.

questions.explanation: On a cylinder, meridians stay parallel instead of converging, so east-west scale increases toward the poles and areas inflate. The landmasses themselves are not larger.
questions.hint: Meridians do not converge on a cylinder.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Great-circle distance and the rhumb-line contrast
questions.learningObjective: Contrast great-circle and rhumb-line routes
questions.stem: Nurse 10 compares a great circle and a rhumb line on a globe.

options.text: A rhumb line is always the shortest route.
options.misconception: confuses rhumb line with great circle

options.text: A great circle is the shortest surface route.
Both lines have equal length on a sphere.
A great circle crosses every meridian at one angle.
options.misconception: confuses great circle with rhumb line

questions.explanation: A great circle is the shortest path between two points on a sphere. A rhumb line crosses meridians at a constant angle and is easier to steer but longer.
questions.hint: Shortest path on a sphere is a great circle.

questions.topic: Cell count of a digital elevation model
questions.learningObjective: Compute DEM cell count from dimensions and resolution
questions.stem: Nurse 11 counts cells in a 2 km by 3 km DEM at 100 m resolution.

options.text: The grid contains 60 cells in total.
The grid contains 6,000 cells in total.
The grid contains 600 cells in total.
The grid contains 6 cells in total.

questions.explanation: Twenty cells across and thirty cells down give 600 cells. Forgetting a dimension or changing resolution gives the wrong counts.
questions.hint: Divide each side by resolution, then multiply.

questions.topic: Matching a projection to the job it must do
questions.learningObjective: Match a projection to its task
questions.stem: Nurse 12 must choose a projection for local angle measurements in a small area.

options.text: Use an equal-area projection for bearings.
Use a conformal projection for measuring area.
Use any projection; all are equivalent.
Use a conformal projection for local angles.

questions.explanation: Conformal projections preserve local angles, so they suit bearing and shape work. Equal-area suits area comparison, and no projection suits every task.
questions.hint: Match the preserved property to the task.

questions.topic: Datums and the offsets they cause
questions.learningObjective: Explain datum offsets
questions.stem: Nurse 13 notices coordinates shift by several metres between two datums.

options.text: Different datums can shift positions by metres.
Datums only change map colours and symbols.
All datums give identical coordinates.
Datum shifts affect only elevation values.

questions.explanation: Datums define the reference frame, so changing datum can shift horizontal or vertical positions by metres. They are not just symbols or elevation-only factors.
questions.hint: A datum is a reference frame, not a symbol.

questions.topic: Geodetic and projected coordinates
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish geodetic and projected coordinates
questions.stem: Nurse 14 compares latitude and longitude with grid eastings and northings.

options.text: Projected coordinates are angles on the ellipsoid.
Geodetic coordinates are angles; projected are planar lengths.
Both are identical measurements in different units.
Projected coordinates include height only.

questions.explanation: Geodetic coordinates are angles on the ellipsoid, while projected coordinates are planar lengths produced by a projection. They are not the same measurement.

questions.explanation: RMSE describes typical error magnitude, not a maximum or a scale. Doubling it gives a rough ninety-five percent bound, not halving.

questions.explanation: A triangulation point is a known, stable point used to measure angles in a survey network. It is not merely a landmark, boundary, or compass reference.

Use the local vertical datum for heights.

questions.explanation: Heights need a consistent vertical datum, preferably the local one, so levels refer to the same reference surface. Horizontal datums or arbitrary choices break comparisons.

questions.topic: Reading the property a projection preserves
questions.learningObjective: Identify projection from a passage

stimulus.body: A handover note describes a projection that preserves local angles and small shapes. It is being used for a small-area bearing survey. Area accuracy is not required.

questions.stem: Nurse 45 identifies the projection property.

options.text: Conformal keeps local shapes.
Equal-area keeps sizes.
Equidistant keeps all distances.
Azimuthal keeps directions.

questions.explanation: Preserving local angles and shapes defines a conformal projection. The other properties belong to different projections.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Area error of a conformal projection at a stated latitude
questions.learningObjective: Explain area error from a passage

stimulus.body: A Mercator map is used in a handover to compare ward catchments. Greenland appears larger than South America. The map is conformal and cylindrical.

questions.stem: Nurse 46 explains the area error.

options.text: Conformal keeps area true everywhere.
Conformal keeps angles, so area distorts.
Conformal keeps distances along parallels.
Conformal removes distortion at the equator.

questions.explanation: Conformal preservation of angles forces area to stretch, especially at high latitudes on a cylinder. Area is not preserved.
questions.hint: Angles preserved force area to change.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: What a conformal projection promises
questions.learningObjective: State conformal promise from a passage

stimulus.body: A handover note explains that a conformal projection is used for local shape fidelity. It does not claim to preserve area. Distances may be distorted away from standard lines.

questions.stem: Nurse 47 states what conformal promises.

options.text: It preserves area across the map.
It preserves distance along every line.
It preserves local angles and shapes.
It preserves direction from one centre.

questions.explanation: The conformal promise is local angle and shape preservation. It does not promise area or global distance.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: What an equal-area projection gives up
questions.learningObjective: State equal-area sacrifice from a passage

stimulus.body: An equal-area projection is chosen in a handover to compare population densities. Shape fidelity is not required. The projection keeps every region's area proportional to reality.

questions.stem: Nurse 48 states what equal-area gives up.

options.text: It keeps both area and shape.
It keeps area, distorts angles only at poles.
It keeps area, stretches distances uniformly.
It keeps area, distorts shape and angle.

questions.explanation: Equal area preserves area but distorts shape, angle, and distance, especially far from standard lines. No projection avoids all distortion.
questions.hint: Equal area costs shape and angle.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Why a cylindrical projection inflates high latitudes
questions.learningObjective: Explain cylindrical inflation from a passage

stimulus.body: A cylindrical projection is used for a world map in a handover. Meridians are drawn parallel. Greenland looks larger than Brazil. The scale is true only along the equator.

questions.stem: Nurse 49 explains high-latitude inflation.

options.text: East-west stretching at high latitudes.
The scale bar is printed too small.
High latitudes are genuinely larger.
Area is preserved, so shapes stretch.

questions.explanation: Parallel meridians prevent convergence, stretching east-west distances and inflating area near the poles. The landmasses are not larger.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Great-circle distance and the rhumb-line contrast
questions.learningObjective: Contrast routes from a passage

stimulus.body: A handover compares two routes between ports. One is a great circle and the other a rhumb line. The great circle crosses meridians at varying angles. The rhumb line keeps a constant bearing.

questions.stem: Nurse 50 compares routes.

options.text: The rhumb line is the shortest route.
options.misconception: confuses rhumb line with great circle

options.text: The great circle is the shortest route.
Both routes have equal length.
The great circle crosses meridians at one angle.
options.misconception: confuses great circle with rhumb line

questions.explanation: A great circle is the shortest surface path. A rhumb line keeps a constant bearing but is longer.
questions.hint: Shortest path is a great circle.

questions.topic: Cell count of a digital elevation model
questions.learningObjective: Compute cells then area
questions.stem: Nurse 51 first counts cells, then converts to area for a 1 km by 2 km DEM at 100 m.

options.text: 200 cells but only 1 sq km.
100 cells covering 2 sq km.
200 cells covering 2 sq km.
2,000 cells covering 2 sq km.

questions.explanation: Ten by twenty cells gives 200 cells over 2 square kilometres. Using the wrong resolution or dimension gives the other counts.

questions.topic: Matching a projection to the job it must do
questions.learningObjective: Match projection then check property
questions.stem: Nurse 52 first picks a projection, then checks its property for bearing work.

options.text: Equal-area for bearings.
Conformal for area.
Any projection works.
Conformal for local angles.

questions.explanation: Conformal preserves local angles, so it suits bearing work. Equal-area suits area comparison, and no projection suits every task.
questions.hint: Match the preserved property to the task.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Datums and the offsets they cause
questions.learningObjective: Explain datum offset then apply
questions.stem: Nurse 53 first explains a datum offset, then applies it to a coordinate.

options.text: Datum shifts positions by metres.
Datum changes colours only.
All datums are identical.
Datum affects elevation only.

questions.explanation: Datums define reference frames, so changing datum can shift positions by metres. They are not just symbols or elevation-only factors.
questions.hint: A datum is a reference frame.

questions.topic: Geodetic and projected coordinates
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish coordinates then convert
questions.stem: Nurse 54 first distinguishes coordinate types, then converts between them.

options.text: Projected coordinates are angles.
Geodetic angles, projected lengths.
Both are identical.
Projected coordinates are height only.

questions.explanation: Geodetic coordinates are angles on the ellipsoid, while projected coordinates are planar lengths. They require a projection to convert.

questions.topic: Linear error of closure of a traverse
questions.learningObjective: Compute precision then interpret
questions.stem: Nurse 55 first computes closure error, then interprets its precision.

options.text: The relative precision is 1:100.
The relative precision is 1:10,000.
The relative precision is 1:1,000.
The relative precision is 1:400.

questions.explanation: Dividing error by total length gives 0.001, or 1:1,000. Misplacing decimals or using the wrong denominator gives other values.

questions.topic: The purpose of a control point
questions.learningObjective: State purpose then apply
questions.stem: Nurse 56 first states the purpose of a control point, then uses it in a survey.

options.text: It stores the map legend.
It marks a boundary only.
It names a landmark.
It provides a known position for surveys.

questions.explanation: A control point anchors measurements with a known position. It is not a legend, boundary, or name.

questions.topic: Reading a stated positional accuracy figure
questions.learningObjective: Interpret accuracy then apply
questions.stem: Nurse 57 first interprets an RMSE, then applies it to a dataset.

options.text: Typical point errors are about the RMSE.
Every point is exactly the RMSE.
Ninety-five percent within half the RMSE.
The map scale is 1:RMSE.

questions.explanation: RMSE describes typical error magnitude, not a maximum or a scale. Doubling gives a rough ninety-five percent bound.

questions.topic: The role of a triangulation point
questions.learningObjective: State role then apply
questions.stem: Nurse 58 first states the role of a triangulation point, then uses it in a network.

options.text: It is only a hiking landmark.
It is a known point for angle measurements.
It marks a property corner.
It records magnetic declination.

questions.explanation: A triangulation point is a known, stable point for measuring angles in a survey network. It is not merely a landmark or boundary.

questions.topic: Choosing a datum for a level run
questions.learningObjective: Choose datum then justify
questions.stem: Nurse 59 first chooses a datum for a level run, then justifies the choice.

options.text: Use a global datum for height only.
Use any datum; heights are absolute.
Use the local vertical datum for heights.
Use a projected datum for elevation.

questions.explanation: Heights need a consistent vertical datum, preferably the local one, so levels refer to the same reference surface.

questions.topic: What a cadastral parcel records
questions.learningObjective: State parcel content then apply
questions.stem: Nurse 60 first states what a cadastral parcel records, then uses it in a visit.

options.text: It records the owner's medical history.
It stores only the parcel area.
It lists the soil type only.
It records boundaries, ownership, and rights.

questions.explanation: A cadastral parcel records spatial boundaries, ownership, and legal rights. It is not a health, soil, or area-only record.
